newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland police chief urges restraint in parades.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland police chief urges restraint in parades.

text.p: Northern Ireland's police chief appealed to the leaders of divided Catholic and Protestant communities on Thursday to use their power to head off the threat of violence at flashpoint Orange Order parades.

"Everyone of any influence whatever should do all that they can to urge restraint. That is what people of influence should be doing from now to right through Saturday," Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) police chief Ronnie Flanagan told reporters.

He was speaking at a meeting of leaders of the centuries-old Orange Order, whose plans to mark the climax of its annual marching season with Belfast and Londonderry parades on Saturday risk being swamped by Catholic protest.

There was no sign that the Orange Order would bow to appeals from Catholic leaders and the Irish government to voluntarily reroute or postpone their parades to avoid a repeat of the violence which flared after a similar march last Sunday.

Heads of Catholic Residents associations in Belfast and Northern Ireland's second city, Londonderry, have called for mass demonstrations on Saturday to protest against what they say are exhibitions of sectarian triumphalism on their doorsteps.

Flanagan's appeal was directed at both the 60 percent pro-British Protestant majority and 40 percent Catholic minority as the clock ticked towards parades on Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road and to the city centre of Irish nationalist Londonderry.
For Orangemen, Saturday is the "glorious" 12th of July, the climax of an annual marching season when Orangemen hold parades to mark a 1690 Protestant battle victory over a Catholic King.
More than 400 British troops were on their way to Northern Ireland to reinforce the 18,000 aleady in the province and 12,000-strong police in case of renewed violence.
Gerard Rice, head of the Lower Ormeau Road residents, told a news conference he expected Catholics to protest in mass and said: "There will be no Orange feet on the Lower Ormeau Road."
In Londonderry, the Bogside residents association chief, Donncha Mac Niallais, told a news conference that he wanted Catholics to protest in huge numbers against parades.

Saturday's Londonderry Orange Order march in the city does not pass through the staunchly Catholic Bogside, but he said "the nationalist community has an absolute right to engage in non-violent protest against sectarian triumphalism."
His aides believe their protest could attract up to 80,000 Catholics. Rice has urged all Irish nationalists to descend on Belfast if the march goes ahead.

The Orange Order says it is being wrongly blamed for the violence which flared after Sunday's march along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown and wants only to hold peaceful marches to celebrate its Protestant faith and British loyalty.
Flanagan said he would continue to hold meetings with those involved in the weekend parades but gave no sign of any early breakthrough that would ease tension.

A spate of car hijackings, riots and petrol bomb attacks on police and troops dwindled overnight but police fear the potential for a fresh flare-up is immense. "I get the feeling it is only half time," one security source said.

Pro-British Loyalist gunmen ratcheted up tension by accusing Irish Republican Army guerrillas of shooting into Protestant areas in nightly unrest and intimidating Protestant families living close to Catholic zones.
The outlawed Ulster Freedom Fighters said in a message to Belfast media that it would "defend" Protestant families and warned IRA gunmen to accept the consequences of their action.

No-one has been killed in the violence that flared after last Sunday's Garvaghy Road parade but gunmen from the IRA and allied groups opposed to British rule of the province have tried to ambush security patrols, slightly injuring two police.
To date 60 police and 64 civilians have been injured. Some 2,500 plastic bullets have been fired and 133 people have been arrested, according to the latest RUC tally.
